name: Manka Longshan Temple
address: No. 211, Guangzhou St, Wanhua District, Taipei City
description: The only pair of bronze dragon pillars in all of Taiwan stands right before the main hall of Manka Longshan Temple, one of the oldest temples in Taipei's Wanhua District — here, even the columns holding up the roof are something you won't find anywhere else. Step into the three-hall, courtyard-enclosed complex and look up: the main hall's spiral caisson ceiling coils inward ring by ring, astonishing in its detail. Longshan Temple's main hall is dedicated to Guanyin Bodhisattva, yet its rear hall houses more than a hundred deities — Mazu, Wenchang Dijun, Lord Guan (Guansheng Dijun), and the beloved Matchmaker (Yue Lao) among them — packing all of the Taiwanese 'no divide between gods and buddhas' spirit into a single temple, where you can pray for success, love, or peace, each at its own altar. It ranks alongside Taipei 101 and the National Palace Museum as a must-see for international visitors, but to the people of Wanhua it is simply the neighborhood temple they come to on the 1st and 15th of every lunar month. Stone carving, woodwork, and painted decoration fill every corner, and at the height of worship the entire forecourt fills with people.
history: In 1738, during the Qianlong reign of the Qing dynasty, a group of immigrants from the Three Districts of Quanzhou crossed the strait to Taiwan and brought a divided incense of Guanyin from their hometown's Longshan Temple in Jinjiang to Manka, building this temple. In its early days it was far more than a place of worship — it served as a center where immigrants met and settled affairs, and even became a historical stage during the Qing-era 'Ding-Xia Jiao Feud' between clan factions. Over more than two centuries, earthquakes, storms, and war struck again and again. The most harrowing came near the end of World War II, when Allied air raids destroyed the main hall completely — yet afterward people found the Guanyin statue unharmed, a wonder devotees still recount as Longshan's 'greatest miracle.' The temple we see today is largely the work of the master craftsman Wang Yi-shun, who led its meticulous restoration in the 1920s, turning this temple reborn from disaster into a masterpiece of traditional Taiwanese temple architecture.

name: Xingtian Temple
address: No. 109, Minquan E. Rd. Sec. 2, Zhongshan District, Taipei City
description: In other temples incense smoke hangs thick in the air; inside Xingtian Temple you won't catch a single wisp. This 'Enzhugong Temple' in Taipei's Zhongshan District was a pioneer — back in 2014 it banned incense and the burning of joss paper entirely, asking worshippers simply to press their palms together in prayer. Dedicated to Guansheng Dijun (Lord Guan), it does everything the opposite way: no donation boxes, no animal offerings, only the belief that 'sincerity, not offerings, moves the gods.' The architecture is imposing yet so plain it is almost free of ornate carving, which only deepens its solemnity. What stays with visitors most are the blue-robed volunteers: when the mind is unsettled or fortunes are low, many come to line up for their 'soul-calming' (shoujing) rite, seeking a measure of peace for body and spirit.
history: The story of Xingtian Temple begins with a lay devotee named Huang Cong, whom followers revered as 'Master Xuan Kong.' He vowed to build a temple to Guansheng Dijun, and only after three separate construction efforts did the present temple rise on this site in 1967. Compared with the many centuries-old temples around it, Xingtian is young, yet its rigorous management and reputation for answered prayers soon made it one of the most visited temples in northern Taiwan. Master Xuan Kong gave away his entire fortune to build it and laid down many rules urging people toward goodness — the most far-reaching being the 2014 decision to lead the way in banning incense and joss paper, replacing the traditional smoke with pressed palms and sparking an environmental movement among Taiwan's temples. As for the famous 'soul-calming' service, it still draws crowds every single day, and has become Xingtian Temple's most vivid everyday sight.

name: Dalongdong Baoan Temple
address: No. 61, Hami St, Datong District, Taipei City
description: A temple can win an international award simply for how well it was restored — and Dalongdong Baoan Temple did exactly that. This old temple in Taipei's Datong District insisted on traditional craftsmanship during its restoration rather than the shortcuts of modern quick-fix materials, and in 2003 it earned a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award for Culture Heritage Conservation, becoming a model for temple restoration in Taiwan. It is dedicated to the medicine god Baosheng Dadi, and its walls carry murals by the national-treasure master Pan Li-shui, alongside exquisite Koji pottery and wood carving. With less of the clamor of an ordinary temple and more of a scholarly grace, walking in feels like stepping into a quiet hall of art.
history: In 1742, during the Qianlong reign, immigrants from Tongan brought a divided incense of Baosheng Dadi from the Baijiao Ciji Temple in Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian, to Dalongdong — at first only a small wooden shrine. As the Dalongdong area prospered, the temple was expanded again and again: rebuilt in 1805 as a three-hall stone temple, then refined through the Jiaqing and Daoguang eras into the layout we see today. What truly spread Baoan Temple's fame was the seven-year restoration from 1995 to 2002 — the temple insisted on traditional methods, repairing brick by brick, and the result won the 2003 UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award for Culture Heritage Conservation. Its annual 'Baosheng Cultural Festival' still preserves the 'Fire Lion' rite found nowhere else in Taiwan — a blaze of firelight to drive off evil and pray for blessings, a rare and precious folk tradition.

name: Taipei Xia-Hai City God Temple
address: No. 61, Dihua St. Sec. 1, Datong District, Taipei City
description: How do you fit more than 600 deity statues into a temple smaller than 150 square meters? The Xia-Hai City God Temple on Dihua Street in Taipei's Dadaocheng does just that — the most densely packed temple in Taiwan, yet with astonishing devotion. It is dedicated to the City God (Chenghuang), guardian of the community, but what really draws young people to queue is the Matchmaker (Yue Lao) here. Said to bring together more than 6,000 couples a year, this little temple has become the acknowledged most effective place in Taiwan to pray for love. Don't rush off after praying — remember to drink a cup of the temple's 'Peace Tea,' brewed from red dates, wolfberries, and wedding candy, sweet as a wish for a sweet and lasting union.
history: In 1856, during the Xianfeng reign, a group of Tongan people in Dadaocheng pooled their money to build this City God temple to protect the peace of their settlement. Those were the years when Dadaocheng was taking off on the tea trade, and the temple naturally became the spiritual center for Tongan merchants. Under Japanese rule it once faced demolition, and only the determined efforts of local gentry saved the little temple. The real turning point came in the 1970s, when the temple began promoting worship of the Matchmaker (Yue Lao); wave after wave of people seeking love poured in, and this temple of under 150 square meters leapt to become one of the most popular Yue Lao temples in all Taiwan. Meanwhile the annual 'Taipei City God Reception' on the 13th day of the 5th lunar month packs the streets so tightly it is nicknamed 'the 13th of May, people watching people,' and for a century it has remained one of Taipei's three great temple festivals.

name: Songshan Ciyou Temple
address: No. 761, Bade Rd. Sec. 4, Songshan District, Taipei City
description: Finish praying to Mazu, turn around, and you're in one of Taiwan's liveliest night markets — this is Songshan Ciyou Temple, known as the 'Songshan Mazu Temple,' standing beside the Raohe Street Night Market in Taipei's Songshan District and the most classic model of Taiwan's 'temple-gate' culture. The six-story temple gleams with gold, and the twin dragons chasing a pearl in cut-porcelain (jiannian) work along its roof are dazzlingly fine, more brilliant still when lit at night. It is dedicated to the compassionate and efficacious Black-Faced Mazu, with the Birth-Registration Goddess and Tiger General enshrined alongside. Light your incense, make your wish, then step straight into the Raohe night market next door for a full round of food — one trip that takes in both everyday Taiwanese life and folk faith at once.
history: In 1753, during the Qianlong reign, a mendicant monk named Lin Shou-yi raised funds far and wide to build Ciyou Temple. Songshan was then still called 'Xikou,' an important transshipment port on the Keelung River, and this temple was the shared spiritual center for the residents of thirteen surrounding villages. Under Japanese rule Ciyou Temple underwent a major renovation that added much fine stone and wood carving; after World War II it was rebuilt several more times, its layout growing ever grander. From river-trade hub to railway station town to today's modern commercial district, Xikou changed many times over, and Ciyou Temple witnessed it all. To this day, the 'Ciyou Temple gate' remains the most familiar landmark in the daily life of Songshan's people.

name: Zhinan Temple
address: No. 115, Wanshou Rd, Wenshan District, Taipei City
description: 'Couples who visit Zhinan Temple together will break up' — this most widely told urban legend refers to the 'Immortal Lu Temple' at the foot of Zhinan Mountain in Muzha, Taipei's Wenshan District. Long hailed as the 'foremost sacred mountain under heaven,' Zhinan Temple is a renowned Taoist holy site and a rare temple where Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism are worshipped as one. Built into the mountainside, grand and commanding, it looks out over the entire Taipei Basin from its halls. Within, from the Chunyang Hall dedicated to Lu Dongbin (Patriarch Lu) and the Lingxiao Hall of the Jade Emperor to the Mahavira Hall and the Dacheng Hall, immortals, buddhas, and sages are all gathered on one mountain. As for the break-up legend, devotees have long since turned it around: today it is known as a powerful place to sever bad romances and pray for true love — those wanting to clear the slate and start over make the climb on purpose.
history: In 1882, during the Guangxu reign, Wang Bin-lin, the county magistrate of Tamsui, proposed building Zhinan Temple, at first only a small shrine to Lu Dongbin (Patriarch Lu). Generation after generation expanded it: the Lingxiao Hall was added in the Taisho era under Japanese rule, and after the war the Dacheng Hall (Confucian) and Mahavira Hall (Buddhist) followed, slowly growing into the grand three-teachings-in-one complex of today. Built into the mountain and looking down from on high, reached by more than a thousand stone steps beneath towering ancient trees, it earned the name 'foremost sacred mountain under heaven.' As for the folk saying that Lu Dongbin is strict about matters of the heart and will break up couples who visit together — pure nonsense, yet by a quirk of fate it became the most widely known tale attached to Zhinan Temple.

name: Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple
address: No. 160-1, Ln. 399, Sec. 2, Xingnan Rd, Zhonghe District, New Taipei City
description: A Tudigong statue 109 feet tall stands on the hilltop, gazing down over all of Zhonghe — this is Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple, one of the most famous places in northern Taiwan to pray for wealth, and the most striking landmark in New Taipei's Zhonghe District. The tallest Earth God statue in Taiwan, kindly-faced, holds a gold ingot steady in its hands. The temple sits atop Nanshijiao Mountain with a sweeping view, so a visit takes in the whole panorama of Greater Taipei by night. Open 24 hours, it grows livelier the later it gets — many salespeople and business owners make a habit of climbing up after dark to exchange 'Money Mother' coins and stroke the ingots, praying for their fortunes to flourish.
history: During the Qianlong reign (around the 1770s), Zhangzhou immigrants brought a divided incense of Tudigong from the Erxuan Temple in Nanjing, Fujian; at first it was only a simple straw altar, rebuilt in stone in the Jiaqing era. The name 'Honglu-di' — 'brazier ground' — is no accident: the terrain here resembles a fire brazier in feng shui, and though the elevation is modest the view is superb, earning a feng shui master's praise as a rare 'wealth-gathering point.' That is exactly why Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple became the most famous 'wealth-seeking' Earth God temple in Taiwan. At year's end and the new year, and on the Earth God's birthday on the 2nd day of the 2nd lunar month, the stream of pilgrims and cars up the mountain never ends. The kindly Tudigong statue on the summit, ingot in hand, has long been a landmark of Zhonghe; and after dark, the glittering lights of the Taipei Basin below have made this a celebrated spot for night views as well.

name: Taipei Confucius Temple
address: No. 275, Dalong St., Datong Dist., Taipei City
description: In the main hall of Taipei Confucius Temple you will not find a single statue — this most important Confucian temple in northern Taiwan, in Taipei's Datong District, follows the ancient Confucian teaching against idol worship, honoring the Great Sage and First Teacher Confucius with spirit tablets alone. Modeled on the regulations of the original Confucius Temple in Qufu, Shandong, it is built in the Minnan style, every brick and column upright and solemn. What is most worth a special trip is the annual Confucius Ceremony (the Shidian rite) on Teacher's Day, September 28th — the city mayor serves as chief officiant, dancers perform the Eight-Row Dance (Bayi), and Confucius is honored with the most ancient of rites, Taiwan's most representative celebration of Confucian culture.
history: Taipei's earliest Confucius temple was built in 1879 during the Guangxu reign, but was demolished under Japanese rule. The temple we see today was rebuilt on the initiative of Taipei's gentry beginning in 1925 — they engaged Wang Yi-shun, the famed Quanzhou master who designed Longshan Temple, and the work was not completed until 1939. Also built in the Minnan style, it stands in graceful counterpoint to the Dalongdong Baoan Temple just across the wall — one Confucian, one Taoist — together forming the most complete surviving cluster of traditional architecture in Taipei.

name: Taipei Wenchang Temple
address: No. 9, Ln. 45, Minsheng W. Rd., Zhongshan Dist., Taipei City
description: When exam season arrives, the walls of Taipei Wenchang Temple fill with photocopies of exam admission tickets, layered densely into a remarkable sight. This temple beside Shuanglian MRT station in Taipei's Zhongshan District is the most visited Wenchang temple in the city center, dedicated to Wenchang Dijun, the deity who governs scholarly success. Worshippers arrive carrying bags of 'homophone offerings' — scallions (cong) for cleverness, celery (qin) for diligence, radish (caitou) for good fortune, and rice dumplings (zongzi) for a 'guaranteed pass' — pinning all their hopes for exam success onto these tangible tokens of intent.
history: Taipei Wenchang Temple was founded during the Guangxu reign of the Qing dynasty (around the 1870s), at first a place where scholars and literati of the Dalongdong area worshipped Wenchang Dijun; together with Baoan Temple and the Confucius Temple, it formed the cultural and religious core of Dalongdong. Under Japanese rule it was briefly relocated for urban planning, then later moved back to its present site. It has been renovated many times, and though modest in scale its architecture is refined and elegant. Set in central Taipei with easy access, and buoyed by years of a reputation for answered prayers, it gradually became a must-visit Wenchang temple for students from across Taiwan. On the eve of major exams the temple fills with candidates and parents praying for success, and that wall papered with admission tickets, along with the temple's 'wisdom brush,' has become a one-of-a-kind cultural sight.

name: Songshan Fengtian Temple
address: No. 12, Ln. 221, Fude St., Xinyi Dist., Taipei City
description: The moment midnight strikes on the 9th day of the first lunar month, Songshan Fengtian Temple is packed shoulder to shoulder with worshippers come to 'pay respects to the Heavenly Lord' — the grandest night of the whole year. This Taoist temple in Taipei's Xinyi District is dedicated to the Jade Emperor, the Heavenly Lord, and is one of the most important centers of Jade Emperor worship in the Taipei area. The gleaming golden main hall enshrines the Jade Emperor, flanked by the Three Officials and the Star Lords of the Northern and Southern Dippers. To see how Taiwanese people honor Heaven with the most solemn of rites, the 'Heavenly Lord's Birthday' on the 9th is the most spectacular lesson — the full 'five-offering' sacrifice laid out in a scene said to be the largest in Taipei.
history: Songshan Fengtian Temple was founded during the Guangxu reign of the Qing dynasty (around the 1880s), at first only a simple straw altar where local residents came to worship the Heavenly Lord. As followers grew year by year, and through repeated expansions from the Japanese era into the postwar period, it reached its present scale. The major reconstruction of the 1960s was the most decisive — the temple deliberately modeled its main hall on Minnan palace-style architecture, building it gleaming with gold and towering in grandeur. The incense at its Heavenly Lord censer has always burned strong, and especially on the 'Heavenly Lord's Birthday' on the 9th of the first lunar month, worshippers pour in from midnight bearing the most solemn five-offering sacrifice — a scale of worship said to be the greatest in Taipei. As the Xinyi District developed and the crowds grew, Songshan Fengtian Temple secured its place as one of the most important centers of Jade Emperor worship in the Taipei area.

name: Keelung Dianji Temple
address: No. 27-2, Ren 3rd Rd, Ren'ai District, Keelung City
description: One of Taiwan's most famous night markets grew up around a single temple — this is the wonder of Keelung Dianji Temple. Standing in Keelung's Ren'ai District, it is one of the 'three great temples of Keelung,' dedicated to Kaizhang Shengwang, and the entire 'Keelung Miaokou (Temple-Gate) Night Market' fans outward from it, creating the singular scene of 'a night market within the temple, a night market ringing the temple.' It is at once a center of faith and a food destination famous across Taiwan, its incense and its crowds never fading year-round. Don't only mind the food — look up at the carved beams and painted rafters, especially that pair of masterfully carved stone dragon pillars.
history: In 1875, the first year of the Guangxu reign, Lin Wei-yuan of the Lin family of Banqiao donated the land and helped build Dianji Temple, dedicated to Kaizhang Shengwang, making it the most important center of Zhangzhou faith in the Keelung area. From the First Sino-Japanese War through the Japanese colonial period, Dianji Temple underwent many major renovations, its fate bound tightly to Keelung's own — from Qing-era trading port to later international harbor, it witnessed all the rise and change of Keelung Harbor. The temple still preserves many precious Qing-dynasty plaques and stone stelae recording the pioneering stories of Keelung's early settlers. And the temple-gate night market around it, running unbroken from the Japanese era to today, has long become Keelung's most iconic tourist landmark.

name: Hsinchu City God Temple
address: No. 75, Zhongshan Rd, North District, Hsinchu City
description: In rank, Hsinchu City God Temple is the highest-ranking City God temple in all Taiwan — a claim backed by the 'Jinmen Baozhang' plaque bestowed by the Qing Guangxu Emperor himself. This old temple in Hsinchu's North District burns with devotion, and its most stirring scene comes at the 'Hsinchu Zhongyuan City God Festival' in the 7th lunar month: in the 'bearing the cangue' (hangjia) rite, tens of thousands of worshippers parade through the streets wearing paper cangues in penance, a spectacular sight. After paying respects to the City God, don't miss the famous street food ringing the temple square — meatballs (gongwan), rice noodles, and pork balls stall after stall, a place where faith and food are satisfied at once.
history: In 1748, during the Qianlong reign, Zeng Ri-ying, the sub-prefect of Tamsui, proposed building the Hsinchu City God Temple, one of the oldest government-built temples in the Hsinchu area. In the Qing imagination the City God temple was like an 'underworld county yamen,' facing the yamen of Hsinchu's magistrate from afar — one of the netherworld, one of the living — symbolizing the ideal of 'gods and people governing together.' It was rebuilt many times through the Jiaqing and Guangxu reigns, and under Japanese rule the gentleman Zheng Zhao-ji led a large-scale renovation that set its layout as it stands today. The temple preserves a great many Qing plaques and couplets, the 'Li Yang Qi' plaque being the most famous. Its annual 'City God Procession' is the largest religious event in Hsinchu City, and the route by which the City God circles the four city gates — north, south, east, and west — has continued for nearly three hundred years. The temple-front square and its surrounding stalls have grown into the renowned 'City God Temple-Gate' food street.

name: Taoyuan Jingfu Temple
address: No. 208, Zhongzheng Rd, Taoyuan District, Taoyuan City
description: When people in Taoyuan say they're 'going to the big temple to pray,' they mean Jingfu Temple — this municipal historic site in Taoyuan District is the most important center of faith in the whole city center. Dedicated to Kaizhang Shengwang, it also brings together the beliefs of both the Zhangzhou and Quanzhou immigrants of this region, a single temple inscribed with the history of ethnic integration. Limited by the tight urban land, Jingfu Temple developed a distinctive 'hip-and-gable with false four-slope' roof, tiers rising one upon another for an especially magnificent silhouette. It sits right on the traffic roundabout at the heart of Taoyuan, a spiritual landmark the city's people need only look up to see.
history: During the Jiaqing reign (around the 1810s), immigrants from Zhangzhou, Fujian, pooled their funds to build a 'Jingfu Shrine' to Kaizhang Shengwang — the forerunner of today's Jingfu Temple. As Taoyuan gradually developed, the temple expanded along with it, becoming the most important center of faith in the city center. It was renovated many times through the Daoguang and Tongzhi reigns, underwent a large-scale renovation under Japanese rule, was formally renamed 'Jingfu Temple' after the war, and completed its most recent major renovation in 2002, its appearance renewed. From Qing-era pioneer settlement to today's special municipality, Taoyuan has changed and changed again, yet this largest Earth God temple in Taoyuan has always stood at the city center, a spiritual stronghold shared by generations of Taoyuan people.

name: Dharma Drum Mountain
address: No. 555, Fagu Rd., Jinshan Dist., New Taipei City
description: Step into Dharma Drum Mountain and you'll find it looks less like the incense-wreathed temple you might imagine and more like a serene mountain academy. This monastery set among the lush green hills of New Taipei's Jinshan District is one of Taiwan's four major Buddhist organizations, founded by Master Sheng Yen in 1989. Its architecture deliberately blends modern lines with the spirit of Zen, echoing everywhere the Master's ideal of 'protecting the spiritual environment.' The main hall enshrines Shakyamuni Buddha, and the campus also holds a meditation center and a Buddhist college. For anyone wishing to set the clamor aside for a while and learn to still the mind, Dharma Drum Mountain is the most representative place of Taiwanese Buddhism's modernization.
history: In 1989, Master Sheng Yen founded Dharma Drum Mountain in Jinshan, though the grand opening ceremony was not held until 2005. He put forward the ideal of 'uplifting the character of humanity and building a pure land on earth,' holding that Buddhism should not merely chant sutras deep in the mountains but step into society, care for the world, and purify the human heart. And so Dharma Drum Mountain is not only a Buddhist monastery but a comprehensive campus combining education, culture, and charity — a path that has earned it an important place in the international Buddhist community as well.

name: Beipu Citien Temple
address: No. 1, Beipu St, Beipu Township, Hsinchu County
description: The start of Beipu Old Street lies right on the stone-paved forecourt of Citien Temple. This county-designated historic site in Beipu Township, Hsinchu County, is the most representative Hakka center of faith in the whole county and the core landmark of the entire Beipu settlement. Dedicated to Guanyin Bodhisattva, it embodies the classic Hakka tradition of 'Guanyin first.' Its plan approaches the Cantonese-Hakka 'double-hall, two-wing' layout, and the Sanchuan Hall is distinguished by its sandstone carving; the pair of stone dragon pillars along the entrance colonnade are both carved as 'ascending dragons' coiling upward — a technique rarely seen in Taiwan's temples. Inside are also two sets of '24 Filial Exemplars' stone columns, finely carved and likewise rare across Taiwan. On weekends, follow the forecourt into the old street and the stream of visitors never stops.
history: The origins of Citien Temple are inseparable from the Han Chinese settlement of Beipu. In 1834, during the Daoguang reign, the Cantonese leader Jiang Xiuluan and the Hokkien merchant Zhou Bangzheng jointly formed the 'Jin Guang Fu' reclamation enterprise to open up the southeastern mountains of Hsinchu — and the Guanyin statue enshrined in the temple was, by tradition, personally brought back from mainland China by Jiang Xiuluan. In 1840 Jiang rebuilt it as a wooden temple. In 1874, during the Tongzhi reign, Jiang Xiuluan's eldest grandson Jiang Ronghua carried out another major reconstruction, adding two wings and a front hall and setting the 'two-hall, two-wing, two-side-house' layout of today. During the 'Beipu Incident' of 1907 in the late Guangxu period, Citien Temple even served as an important base, adding a page of far-reaching history to this temple.

name: Baozhong Yimin Temple
address: No. 360, Sec. 3, Yimin Rd., Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County
description: Most temples enshrine deity statues; Yimin Temple venerates a tomb — and this is what makes Baozhong Yimin Temple the most distinctive and moving of all. This temple in Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County, is the head temple of Yimin (Righteous People) faith across Taiwan and the most important spiritual sanctuary of the Taiwanese Hakka community. Its spiritual core is the 'Yimin Tomb' behind the main hall, the burial place of more than 200 Hakka volunteer warriors who died defending their homeland in Qing-dynasty upheavals such as the Lin Shuangwen Rebellion. The 'Bao Zhong' (Praise Loyalty) plaque hanging high in the main hall was bestowed by the Qianlong Emperor. At the annual Yimin Festival on the 20th day of the 7th lunar month, hosted in rotation by fifteen great townships across the Taoyuan-Hsinchu region, the most talked-about event is the 'Divine Pig Competition' — worshippers vie to raise the fattest sacred pig to honor their ancestors in the most abundant way possible.
history: In 1786, during the Qianlong reign, the Lin Shuangwen Rebellion broke out, and Hakka communities around Hsinchu and Taoyuan formed volunteer militias to defend their homes in bloody battle. After the fighting, more than 200 fallen warriors were buried together at Fangliao (today's Xinpu Township). In 1790 the local people pooled their funds to build a temple in their memory, and the Qianlong Emperor bestowed the 'Bao Zhong' plaque — the origin of Yimin Temple. In every later upheaval — the Zhu Yigui and Dai Chaochun uprisings among them — the righteous who died protecting their homeland were also enshrined here. Thus Yimin Temple became the symbolic sanctuary of the Taiwanese Hakka spirit, and its singular form of worship, 'a tomb as a temple,' has always stood apart in Taiwan's religious culture.

name: Xinzhuang Wu Temple
address: No. 340, Xinzhuang Rd, Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City
description: Other temples paint fierce door gods on their gates; the gate panels of Xinzhuang Wu Temple are bare, studded only with 108 door nails — symbols of the Thirty-Six Heavenly Generals and Seventy-Two Earthly Fiends, meaning that Guansheng Dijun's martial prowess is so supreme he needs no door gods to guard him. This temple in Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City, is the oldest Guan Di temple in northern Taiwan and a designated historic site. It witnessed the prosperous era of Xinzhuang's 'forest of a thousand sails' as a port, and to this day preserves many precious old plaques and stele inscriptions, an important relic for the study of Xinzhuang's history.
history: During the Yongzheng reign (around the 1730s), immigrants from Zhangzhou, Fujian, pooled their funds to build Wu Temple, dedicated to the God of War, Lord Guan. Xinzhuang was then the most flourishing port and trading town in northern Taiwan, its harbor crowded with masts and sails, and Wu Temple was where the merchants prayed for thriving business and urged one another toward loyalty and honesty. It was renovated and expanded many times through the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns, and in the Daoguang era it received an official inscribed plaque, formally becoming a temple of the officially recognized sacrificial register. Under Japanese rule this old temple once faced the threat of demolition, and survived only through the determined protection of local gentry. It still holds precious relics — Qing-dynasty stelae, old plaques, and stone lions — quietly witnessing Xinzhuang's century of change from a thriving port to a modern town.

name: Xinzhuang Dizang An
address: No. 84, Zhongzheng Rd, Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City
description: Those fierce, elaborately face-painted 'Guan Jiang Shou' (Officers of the Vanguard) seen at Taiwanese temple festivals originated right here at Xinzhuang Dizang An. This temple in Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City — commonly called the 'Dazhong Temple' — is dedicated to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva and Wen-Wu Dazhong Ye, presiding over the finding of lost items, the settling of lawsuits, and the driving out of evil, and is a vital center of faith in the Xinzhuang area. On the 1st day of the 5th lunar month each year, the 'Great Xinzhuang Worship' (the Dazhong Ye procession), with its distinctive 'night patrol' rite paired with Guan Jiang Shou performance troupes, is one of the most representative temple festivals in northern Taiwan — well worth a special trip to feel that atmosphere at once fearsome and festive.
history: Dizang An was completed in Xinzhuang during the Qianlong reign (around 1757), one of the oldest Ksitigarbha temples in northern Taiwan. Xinzhuang was in its early days an important commercial port in the north, densely populated but often visited by plague and disaster, and Dizang An became a vital place to deliver wandering souls and pray for the community's peace. The Zhongyuan (Ghost Festival) rites of the 7th lunar month are the temple's grandest moment, with the 'Wen-Wu Dazhong Ye procession' and the 'Guan Jiang Shou' troupe performance the most famous — for Xinzhuang is the very birthplace of the Guan Jiang Shou tradition, those fierce-faced officers charged with awing demons and keeping order between the worlds of the living and the dead, now designated an intangible cultural asset of New Taipei City.

name: Hsinchu Sanshan Guowang Temple
address: No. 184, Ximen St., North Dist., Hsinchu City
description: Which three mountains are the Three Mountain Kings? The answer lies in Jin Mountain, Ming Mountain, and Du Mountain in Jieyang, Chaozhou, Guangdong — the mountain gods of these three peaks were the most important guardian deities the Hakka carried across the sea to Taiwan. Built during the Qianlong reign, Hsinchu Sanshan Guowang Temple is the most representative Hakka center of faith in Hsinchu's North District. It preserves many Qing-dynasty plaques and stone carvings that bear witness to the Hakka history of reclaiming the Zhuqian (Hsinchu) region. Built in a traditional blend of Minnan and Cantonese styles, its layout is upright and solemn, and the stone carving of the front hall is especially fine. Though the temple sits in a busy district, the surrounding lanes still keep the grain of the early Hakka settlement, making it the best starting point for understanding Hsinchu's Hakka history.
history: In 1780, during the Qianlong reign, the Cantonese Hakka immigrants of the Hsinchu area pooled their funds to build the Sanshan Guowang Temple. Qing-era Hsinchu once saw severe ethnic conflict between Hokkien and Hakka, and in such times the Sanshan Guowang Temple was not only a place of worship but a vital rallying point where the Hakka drew together and kept alive the ties of kinship and hometown. The temple has been renovated many times yet still preserves the basic layout of its Qing-dynasty architecture. Under Japanese rule it once faced the threat of demolition, and was saved in the end only through the efforts of local people.

name: Hsinchu Putian Temple
address: No. 66, Ln. 306, Gaofeng Rd., East Dist., Hsinchu City
description: Before you even reach Hsinchu Putian Temple, you'll first catch sight of the towering statue of Guansheng Dijun (Lord Guan) rising 120 meters high — grand and imposing, visible from far off, the temple's most famous landmark. This temple in Hsinchu's East District is dedicated to Guansheng Dijun, and being near the Hsinchu Science Park, it is a center of faith for many of the park's tech workers. Beyond Lord Guan, Putian Temple's Matchmaker (Yue Lao) is also well known, drawing many single men and women to pray for a good match — seeking a little guidance for their love lives in this efficiency-driven tech city.
history: Hsinchu Putian Temple was founded during the Daoguang reign of the Qing dynasty (around the 1840s), built with funds raised by Hakka devotees of the Hsinchu area, at first only a small temple. It was renovated and expanded many times thereafter, gradually growing to its present scale. Under Japanese rule the temple was once requisitioned, and was restored by local devotees only after the war. Its architecture is plain yet solemn, and it still preserves some Qing-dynasty stone-carved components. Over the years the temple has continued to run community services and lectures, keeping close ties with the surrounding neighborhood — an important place in the Hsinchu area that serves both religious faith and community cohesion.

name: Hsinchu Puxian Temple
address: No. 536, Sec. 1, Guangfu Rd., East Dist., Hsinchu City
description: In the main hall of Hsinchu Puxian Temple, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva rides a six-tusked white elephant, serene and dignified — the most striking sight of this Buddhist temple in Hsinchu's East District. Dedicated to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, its buildings are quiet and refined, a rare patch of stillness in the city center. In Buddhism, Samantabhadra represents 'Great Practice,' the power to put the Dharma into daily life step by step; so those who come here mostly seek not wealth or fame but the steadiness to advance in practice and fulfill their vows. For anyone wanting to catch a breath amid the rush, Puxian Temple is a good place to sit down.
history: Hsinchu Puxian Temple was founded during the Daoguang reign of the Qing dynasty (around the 1830s), built with funds raised by local gentry, at first only a small Buddhist temple. Through repeated renovations and expansions from the late Qing into the Japanese colonial period, it gradually became an important Buddhist temple in the Hsinchu area. Dedicated to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, it is known for 'practice and vow' — Samantabhadra's Ten Great Vows are the very heart of Mahayana Buddhist practice. Its architecture blends Minnan and Japanese styles, every brick and tile bearing the cultural imprint of a different age. After the war the temple continued to expand, adding a lecture hall and a library and actively promoting Buddhist education and charity. Quiet and shaded by ancient trees, it is a rare place for still cultivation in central Hsinchu.

name: Sanxia Changfu Temple
address: No. 1, Changfu St, Sanxia District, New Taipei City
description: Walk into Sanxia Changfu Temple and don't look up at the statues first — look at the pillars. The birds, flowers, and figures on every stone column were cut by hand, deep enough to slip a finger into. This temple to Qingshui Zushi has been rebuilt since 1947 under the direction of Li Mei-shu, a painter born in Sanxia, who brought the training of Western fine art into a traditional temple and kept at it for decades. He died before the work was finished. That is why Changfu Temple is that rare thing in Taiwan: an old temple still being built, a relay across three generations of craftsmen. It was designated a New Taipei City heritage site in 2018.
history: In 1767, Anxi migrants from Quanzhou settled around Sanxia, Yingge, Shulin, and Daxi and proposed a temple; it was completed two years later, in 1769, enshrining the Qingshui Zushi of their home region. The area was then called Sanjiaoyong, where three rivers meet, and the temple stood at the center of the settlement — a place of worship and a place where migrants settled their affairs. Its transformation came in the twentieth century. In 1947 the painter Li Mei-shu took charge of the rebuilding. He refused to rush; every carving had to be worthy of the temple, and the work stretched across decades. The layered stonework you see today is what that patience left behind.

name: Manka Qingshui Temple
address: No. 81, Kangding Rd, Wanhua District, Taipei City
description: Manka Qingshui Temple is one of the few old temples in Taipei that is only half there. It once had three halls; the rear hall burned in a communal fight and was never rebuilt, so the building simply stops — and that absence became part of its history. Known locally as the Zushi Temple, it enshrines Qingshui Zushi and was funded by Anxi migrants in 1787. It ranks with Longshan Temple and Baoan Temple as one of the "three great temple gates of Taipei," and is a designated city heritage site. Inside it is quieter than you expect: none of Longshan's crowds, light falling through the courtyard, dark timber absorbing half the sound. If you want somewhere in Wanhua to sit for a while, this beats the streets around it.
history: In 1787, Anxi migrants chose Weng You-lai as director and raised thirty thousand silver dollars to build the temple; it was completed in 1790, enshrining a Qingshui Zushi image brought from the original Qingshui Temple in their home county. What changed the temple's fate came in 1853, when fighting broke out in Manka between migrant groups. Fire reached the temple and destroyed it. Believers rebuilt in 1867, but the rear hall was never restored. That unrepaired gap is now the most direct evidence of how Taipei's earliest commercial district grew: out of conflict, and out of rebuilding.

name: Tamsui Qingshui Temple
address: No. 87, Qingshui St, Tamsui District, New Taipei City
description: The Qingshui Zushi enshrined in Tamsui goes by the most vivid name in Taiwan: the Nose-Dropping Ancestor. Legend says that when disaster approaches, the nose of the statue falls off as a warning. It sounds absurd until you hear a Tamsui local tell it — they are entirely serious, because the story is about the survival of a whole town. Built in 1937, the temple is young by local standards, yet it counts among greater Taipei's four great Zushi temples and Tamsui's four great temples. It sits inside the market lanes off Qingshui Street: turn in from the crowded old street and within a few steps the noise gives way to incense smoke. In Tamsui, the busiest and the stillest are one corner apart.
history: Tamsui Qingshui Temple was built in 1937, late compared with other Zushi temples in Taiwan — but the deity it enshrines had been part of Tamsui life far longer than the building. The story of the falling nose circulated in the neighborhood before there was any temple, and believers took turns hosting the image in private homes until the hall was finished and it finally had a fixed address. That sequence — faith first, temple after — is why this place is bound so tightly to the streets around it. Nobody built a temple and waited for worshippers; people believed for decades, then built the temple together. It is now counted among the four great Zushi temples of greater Taipei, alongside those of Manka, Sanxia, and Ruifang.

name: Tamsui Yinshan Temple
address: No. 15, Denggong Rd, Tamsui District, New Taipei City
description: Yinshan Temple will make you rethink what a temple is: the side chambers here were not built for a deity, but for people to sleep in. Founded in 1822 by Hakka migrants from Tingzhou in western Fujian, it enshrines their guardian, Dingguang Gufo, and set aside its two wings as the Tingzhou Guild Hall so that newcomers from home had somewhere to stay the moment they stepped off the boat. Only two Qing-era Dingguang Buddha temples survive in Taiwan; this is the northern one, and the better preserved — two halls, two corridors, two side chambers, now a national heritage site. For those migrants the building was at once the god's home and their own: settle the faith first, then settle the body.
history: In 1822, Hakka migrants from the eight counties of Tingzhou prefecture in western Fujian built Yinshan Temple in Tamsui. They were a relative minority among Taiwan's settlers — different in speech, in origin, and in custom from the Quanzhou and Zhangzhou communities around them — so from the beginning the temple was more than a place of worship. Its side chambers served as the Tingzhou Guild Hall, lodging for countrymen who had just crossed the strait and had nowhere yet to go. The deity in the main hall, the newcomers in the wings: one building taking the word "protection" literally. The layout has barely changed in two hundred years, which is why it stands today as a national heritage site and the best preserved Dingguang Buddha temple in Taiwan.

name: Linkou Zhulinshan Guanyin Temple
address: No. 325, Zhulin Rd, Linkou District, New Taipei City
description: The temple's name is assembled from three places — Luzhu, Linkou, and Guishan, one character each. The naming is honest about what this is: not one village's temple, but a center of faith raised by three communities together. It enshrines the eighteen-armed Guanyin, and the halls completed in the 2012 rebuild used thirty-eight thousand-year-old Taiwanese cypress timbers; what you notice first on entering is the smell of wood, not incense. Outside lies a garden of several hectares, cherry blossoms in spring, and on a weekday morning close to nothing but the sound of someone sweeping — one of the few places near Taipei that manages to be both large and quiet.
history: In 1801, worshippers brought three Guanyin images from the Longshan Temple of Anhai, Jinjiang, in Fujian. At first there was no temple; households across the villages took turns hosting the images. The real test came late in the Japanese colonial period, when the assimilation campaign suppressed Taiwanese folk religion and sought to burn its statues — believers hid the Guanyin and kept worship going in secret. The colonial government eventually permitted a temple in Japanese style, completed at the present site in 1939, and the name was made from one character each of Luzhu, Linkou, and Guishan to record who had protected it together. After study trips abroad, the temple completed its current rebuild in 2012.

name: Manka Dizang Temple
address: No. 245, Xichang St, Wanhua District, Taipei City
description: Manka Dizang Temple is small enough to walk straight past — a single hall three bays wide, wedged between shopfronts on Xichang Street, with no archway and no forecourt. That is precisely what makes it valuable. Most of Taipei's old temples expanded over two centuries; this one kept the form of a mid-Qing single-hall temple, swallowtail ridge, gable walls, and rolled-roof entrance corridor intact. It enshrines Ksitigarbha, with Marshal Tian Du and the City God in attendance. It is not a tourist stop; most days there are only a few old neighbors sitting by the door. If you want to see what a temple originally looked like rather than what restoration made of it, this is Taipei's plainest example.
history: Manka Dizang Temple was built in 1760 and repaired in 1838, making it one of the earliest surviving temples in Taipei. It faced a crisis under Japanese rule, when the authorities moved to bring folk temples into public ownership; to keep the property, the temple transferred management to Manka Longshan Temple, and that arrangement carried it through. Because it was never substantially rebuilt, it preserves the full form of a mid-Qing single-hall temple and is now a designated heritage site. Each year on the thirtieth day of the seventh lunar month, Ksitigarbha's feast day, this quiet little temple holds a large universal deliverance rite — its busiest day of the year, and the way Wanhua remembers it.
